To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) the free market and social engineering are not mutually exclusive; (2) command law and facilitative law are not mutually exclusive either; and (3) contract law is not a facilitative law.

(1) the law of contract in Kenya and Ghana has been and remains facilitative, (2) the free market has not been and is not now the dominant force in these economies, (3) social engineering and planning have been and are now the dominant economic forces in these economies, and (4) state intervention has been and is now a major factor in the development of both economies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between social engineering, the free market, and contract law.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the law of contract has been used in Kenya to support the free market, while in Ghana it has been used to support social engineering.
contract law in Kenya is facilitative, whereas contract law in Ghana is command.
social engineering and the free market are not the opposites that they are frequently assumed to be.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the classical dichotomy between social engineering and the free market is based upon a false assumption about how contract law functions, that is, upon a failure to distinguish the legal expression of contract from the legal expression of the social relations of production.
the law of contract, far from being facilitative, is in many respects a set of commands.
the law of contract, in both theory and practice, is neither a free market nor a command economy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
social engineering is not the opposite of the free market.
social engineering and planning do not beget state power.
contract law, as currently understood, is not a good tool for promoting a free market.
